Known constraints from earlier cycles:
- Keep arithmetic as `base + base * RATE`, NOT `base * (1 + RATE)` — IEEE-754 inexactness breaks a test.
- Do NOT narrow `Item.type` from `string` to a union of known item types.
- Do NOT narrow the `op` fields of QuoteStep/ClaimStep to literal types — verified to break tsc, because the spec builds scenarios in an intermediate `const` which widens `op` to `string`.
- Item-scope surcharges are percentages of the item's OWN base premium; policy-scope modifiers are percentages of the POLICY base premium.
- The policy base must be multiplied exactly once by the netted rate.

Run autonomously, return when done.

27 passing, 22 todo. Now let me evaluate the code for refactoring opportunities.

**Naming Evaluation (First Priority)**

Walking every name in the file against what the code now does:

- `settleClaim`, `payoutForDamage`, `insuranceSumOf`, `policyReferencedBy` — all accurate. `payoutForDamage` is especially good: the newly-confirmed "deductible per damage entry" rule is exactly what that name says, applied once per entry by the reduce in `settleClaim`.
- `INSURANCE_VALUES` / `BASE_PREMIUMS` — the two record names correctly distinguish claim-side sums from quote-side premiums.
- `hasPrecedingStep` — the comment explains precisely why it is named for position rather than contracts. Still correct and still deliberately future-proofed.
- `policyModifiersOn`, `itemSurchargesOf`, `policyBasePremiumOf` — encode the item-scope/policy-scope distinction that the constraints call out as load-bearing.

No rename improves intent here.

**APP Mass — the one candidate I found**

The only structural thing I could see is `groupAlikeItems`, the sole imperative holdout in an otherwise expression-oriented file:

```
for (const item of items) {
  countByType.set(item.type, (countByType.get(item.type) ?? 0) + 1);
}
```

Mass: loop 5 + invocations (set, get, ??) 6 + bindings 3 + constant 1 = 15. A `reduce` version nets out the same (loop 5, plus an extra `.set` return-value chain), so it trades no mass for a less direct read. Rule 2 trumps APP — the `for...of` states "count each item by type" more plainly than a reduce threading a Map accumulator would. I left it.

**Rules 3 and 4**

- Rule 3 (duplication): none. `BASE_PREMIUMS` and `INSURANCE_VALUES` look parallel but are unrelated knowledge — premium pricing vs. claim valuation — and several types appear in one and not the other. Merging them into a single record of `{premium, value}` would couple two independently-changing facts, and the pending "unknown item type" error tests will likely need to distinguish "not insurable" from "not priceable" separately.
- Rule 4 (fewest elements): the small named predicates (`isCursed`, `isHighlyEnchanted`, `isLongStanding`) each cost an invocation over an inline comparison, but each names a domain rule that the spec names. Inlining them would lower mass and lose intent. Keeping them.

**Outcome**

As you anticipated, this cycle was a pure data addition — one row, `amulet: 600`, into an existing lookup table, and the deductible rule that came with it needed no code at all because `settleClaim`'s reduce already had the right shape. There is no new structure to clean up, and I could not find a change to the surrounding code that improves it on any of the four rules without costing clarity.

**No refactoring applied.** The mandatory attempt was made across all four rules and naming; each candidate is documented above with the reason it was rejected. I deliberately did not make a cosmetic change just to have one to report — that would churn a file whose shape is currently doing real work holding the item-scope/policy-scope distinction and the arithmetic-ordering constraints intact.

Verification (state unchanged from when I started, since I edited nothing):

- `pnpm test` — 27 passed, 22 todo, 0 failed
- `npx tsc --noEmit` — clean

One thing worth flagging for the next cycles: `policyReferencedBy` in `/home/experimenter/experiments/runs/2026-08-11_01-43-28_claim-office-example-mapping_v6.6-lab-split-cc_opus-5-no-thinking/src/claim-office.ts` still contains the unchecked cast

```ts
steps[claim.policy] as QuoteStep
```

That is the single isolated place the pending error-handling tests will need to change, and it is already documented as such in the comment above it. Also, `hasPrecedingStep` is currently correct only because every step that precedes a quote in the passing tests happens to be a quote — the pending "cap persistence across multiple claims" tests will interleave claim steps, and at that point the call site in `runScenario` must switch to counting preceding *quote* steps rather than any step.
